clue.text: Break out a little rum, Al -' several parties involved

indicators.note: to break out is to burst free, so the letters of the words that follow are let loose into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone sneaks a drop of rum to Al while a whole crowd of people join in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break out' signals the anagram: A LITTLE RUM rearranges to MULTILATER, and AL is added as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Talks or treaties joining many nations or sides at once are described this way.

clue.text: He runs a horse into the sea in Calais

indicators.note: into tells us the a-plus-horse piece goes inside the French word for sea

parts.note: in French, as spoken at Calais, the sea is la mer
a nag is an old or worn-out horse

explanation.surface: A rider drives a horse into the waves on the beach at Calais.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He runs' looks like the start of the horse story, but it is the definition: a boss runs a business. 'into' signals the container; the sea is given in French because of Calais.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is the person who runs a business, shop or team.

clue.text: Vegetables to stick in the grounds

indicators.note: in shows the word for sticking sits inside the word for the grounds

parts.note: lees are the dregs or grounds that settle at the bottom of a wine cask
to gum something is to stick it, as with glue

explanation.surface: A gardener is told to plant vegetables in the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grounds' suggests soil, but here it means the dregs left in a wine cask; 'in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Peas, beans and lentils are pod-bearing vegetables of this plant family.

clue.text: The end for those on the way to Hell

definitions.text: The end for those on the way to Hell

parts.words: The end for those on the way to Hell
parts.note: an end can be an aim or purpose, and the proverb says the road to hell is paved with good ones

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the road to hell is paved with good intentions' supplies the cryptic hint; 'The end' means a purpose, not a finish.
explanation.definitionFit: An aim or purpose is an end, and the proverb paves the road to hell with good ones.

clue.text: Knowing there's something to sell

definitions.meaning: knowing means informed or conscious of something
goods offered for sale are wares, and one such item is a single article of merchandise

explanation.surface: A shrewd trader knows there is something worth selling.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as two words to get the second sense: one item of goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowing means informed or conscious; split in two, the word gives one article of merchandise.

clue.text: It prohibits English doctor going on ship

parts.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a medical degree standing for a doctor
the Argo was Jason's ship in Greek myth

explanation.surface: A ban stops an English doctor from boarding a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going on' simply joins the pieces, which run in clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: An official ban on trade with a country is a measure that forbids, so it prohibits.

clue.text: Gas machine ventilates the joint

parts.note: airs means ventilates, as when you air a stuffy room
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: A gas-powered device freshens the air in a seedy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joint' suggests a dive or bar, but it is the body's HIP; 'Gas machine' playfully describes a flying craft held up by gas.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirigible is a flying machine held aloft by a lighter-than-air gas.

clue.text: May be ascribed to Butler — a bit at variance

indicators.note: variance means difference or change, so the preceding letters are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A remark could be credited to a butler who is slightly out of step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at variance' reads as one phrase, but 'at' is part of the fodder: BUTLER A BIT AT gives the twelve letters, and 'variance' alone is the anagram signal; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can be credited to a cause or source is ascribable to it.

clue.text: Nearly in' the drink this time!

indicators.note: in places the word for nearly inside the word for a drink

parts.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits
nigh is an old word for near or nearly, as in nigh on

explanation.surface: Someone almost fell into the sea this time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the drink' is slang for the sea, but here it is a small measure of spirits; 'in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: The coming evening of the present day is this time, as opposed to another night.

clue.text: King with a province

parts.note: Albert was the name of kings of the Belgians

explanation.surface: A monarch is handed a province of his own.
explanation.definitionFit: This western Canadian region, capital Edmonton, is one of the country's provinces.

clue.text: Girl has panther imported for sound broadcast

parts.note: Ann is a girl's name
the ounce, or snow leopard, is a big cat, loosely a panther

indicators.note: for sound means the word is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to import is to mean or signify, so imported is meant

explanation.surface: A girl brings in a big cat for a radio show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imported' means signified, MEANT, which 'for sound' turns into its sound-alike MENT; 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcast can be a public statement or news item put out to listeners.

clue.text: Course to form into groups? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite means the word falls just short of complete, losing its final letter

parts.note: to regiment people is to organise them into strict groups or units

explanation.surface: A training course where people are almost sorted into teams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' removes the last letter, T, from REGIMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A prescribed programme of diet, exercise or treatment is a course.

clue.text: Receiver at that time made of clay

parts.note: the ear receives sound, so it is a receiver
then means at that time

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned telephone handset turns out to be made of clay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Receiver' suggests a telephone, but it is the EAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot fashioned from baked soil or clay is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Sounds like.Brooke's a poet

definitions.meaning: Brooke's is said like brook's, and a small Scottish stream is called a burn
a writer of verse, here Scotland's national bard

explanation.surface: Apparently Brooke is a poet, as Rupert Brooke indeed was.
explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Brooke, the First World War poet, is a decoy: his name sounds like brook, and a brook in Scotland is a burn.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert, Scotland's national bard, wrote Auld Lang Syne; a Scottish brook is a burn.

clue.text: Not prepared to make a claim to .be on time you say

parts.note: saying 'I am' claims to be something, shortened to two letters with an apostrophe
prompt means punctual, on time

indicators.note: say signals that the following word is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: you is heard as the single letter U

explanation.surface: Someone who isn't ready insists they will be punctual.
explanation.walkthrough: Claiming to be on time, you say 'I'm prompt'; 'you say' gives U for YOU.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done off the cuff, without rehearsal, is unprepared.

clue.text: "And. -s show untrodden green" (Keats)

parts.note: the line, from Keats's Sleep and Poetry, fills its gap with sheer cliff faces that no foot has trodden

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the blank in the Keats line; the printed '-s' shows the word is used there in the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheer cliff face, too steep for walkers, is the steep drop Keats pictured.

clue.text: Allowable deviation from clear note, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the words could be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: An engineer reads the permitted error off a clearly written note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals the anagram of CLEAR NOTE; 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In engineering, the permitted margin of error in a measurement is this.

clue.text: Archbishop disturbing our inertia

parts.note: Cosmo Lang was Archbishop of Canterbury from 1928 to 1942

indicators.note: disturbing means stirring up, so the letters of our are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A churchman shakes us out of our sluggishness.
explanation.walkthrough: Cosmo LANG was Archbishop of Canterbury 1928-42; 'disturbing' turns OUR into UOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Lethargy or listless sluggishness is a state of inertia.

clue.text: Island gathering

definitions.meaning: a French overseas island department in the Indian Ocean, east of Madagascar
a meeting of old friends or relatives who come together again

explanation.definitionFit: One sense names a French island near Mauritius; the other is a meeting of people who were together before.

clue.text: Numbers relating to a city

definitions.meaning: read as Roman numerals the letters give a string of numbers: a hundred, one, five, one, a hundred
concerning a town or municipality and its citizens

explanation.surface: Statistics about a municipal area.
explanation.walkthrough: Roman numerals are a common trick: any word made of the letters I, V, X, L, C, D, M can be read as numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as Roman numerals the letters are numbers; as a word it means belonging to a municipality or town.

clue.text: Home of this industry

parts.note: small-scale manufacturing done in workers' own houses is named after the small rural dwelling they lived in

explanation.walkthrough: A small-scale trade carried on at home is called a cottage industry, so the home names the industry.
explanation.definitionFit: A small country house gives its name to home-based manufacturing.

clue.text: Victory over the law about the right sentence

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the first piece above the next one

parts.note: V is the abbreviation for victory, as in V-sign or VE Day

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the law word goes round the right

parts.note: an edict is a decree or law
R is the usual abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A triumph against the law over the proper punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts R inside EDICT, giving ERDICT, with V placed 'over' it in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: In the older legal sense a sentence is a judicial decision or judgment pronounced on a case.

clue.text: Feast in urban Quetta

indicators.note: in shows the answer is tucked inside the words urban Quetta

explanation.surface: A lavish feast laid on in the Pakistani city of Quetta.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand formal meal for many guests is a feast.

clue.text: Argument of article about mutton

parts.note: the is the definite article

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the printers' word is read backwards

parts.note: printers call an em space a mutton, to tell it apart from the en, called a nut

explanation.surface: An essay making a point about lamb's older cousin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mutton' is printers' slang for EM, the em quad; 'about' turns it to ME.
explanation.definitionFit: The topic or subject under discussion is the argument of a book or essay.

clue.text: In a word, one is temporary

indicators.note: is reads here as is inside, so the one sits within the phrase in a word

parts.note: a term is a word or expression
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Put briefly, someone's position is only temporary.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as 'one is (inside) In a word': 'is' carries the container sense, and the Roman numeral for one goes inside the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Something provisional, lasting only until a replacement comes, is temporary.

clue.text: Learned of river rising with swirling tide

indicators.note: rising means going up, so the river's name is read backwards

parts.note: the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

indicators.note: swirling means spinning round, so the letters of tide are churned up

explanation.surface: A scholarly study of a river coming up on a turning tide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns URE (a Yorkshire river) into ERU; 'swirling' makes DITE from TIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholarly person with deep book knowledge is well-read, or learned.

clue.text: It has a secure backing as a race

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word for secure is read in reverse

parts.note: to nail something is to fix or secure it

explanation.surface: A secure financial backer puts something in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' signals the reversal of the word for secure; 'has' and 'as a' are links, and 'race' means a people or nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of the nation centred on Rome form a race or nationality.

clue.text: Royal personage put this French variety of green in the picture

indicators.note: in shows the French word and the scrambled green go inside the picture word

parts.note: a print is a picture made from an engraving or photograph
ce is French for this

indicators.note: a variety of something is a different form of it, so the letters of green are rearranged

explanation.surface: A royal tells a French painter to add a kind of green to the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: CE (French 'this') and REGEN (an anagram of GREEN, from 'variety of') go 'in' PRINT; 'put' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: George IV ruled as royal stand-in for his father from 1811 to 1820.
